english.html: led Sanxi, still living: but for some slight theft of wheat, which this Martin had committed against his father, he had absented himself from the country, and remained eight years abroad, without the supplicant, during that time, having heard any news whatever of him.

This long duration and lengthy absence of the husband made him, at first sight, greatly culpable, and almost beyond all excuse, as having given the occasion for the misfortune and disaster which has since followed from it: witness Saint Augustine, when he says, IF YOU abstain for long without the will of your wife, you give her licence to fornicate: and if she goes astray, her sin will be imputed to your abstinence <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>. Whence some have even dared to say that a Judge might justly absolve a wife accused by her husband of adultery, if she is not convicted of having squandered her honour and abandoned herself except after having been long forsaken by her husband <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>; inasmuch as the husband, who has furnished the occasions, and has thereby made himself guilty of the misdeed <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>, cannot upbraid her with it, nor object it against his wife <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. As in a like case also, the husband, who by the old laws could repudiate his consort if without his leave she had slept outside the house <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>, nevertheless, if he himself had driven her out, and on that occasion she remained all night outside, cannot repudiate her, because (says Justinian) he himself is the author of this fault <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. But if this opinion were true, women, licentious enough of themselves, might seize upon a great pretext to prostitute themselves with impunity, covering themselves with the cloak of the husband's absence: to which, so far from our being bound to lend a hand, on the contrary everyone ought to reject this opinion as impious, unworthy of a Christian, and so barbarous that even the Gentiles and Pagans did not think it good that a wife (whose husband had remained long absent) should remarry, until after having heard

notes.citation: Augustine, De adulterinis coniugiis; transcribed in the Decretum Gratiani as c. Si tu abstines, C. 28 q. 2 (as Coras cites it; locus not verified)
notes.original: S. Auguſt au liure De adulterinis cõiugiis, les paroles duquel ſont tranſcrites au c. ſi tu abſtines xxviij. q. ij.
notes.gloss: The words quoted in the text: a husband who abstains against his wife's will answers for her fornication.

notes.citation: Petrus Ravennas (Pierre de Ravenne, Pietro da Ravenna, c. 1448–1508), Alphabetum aureum
notes.original: Pierre de Rauenne en ſon Alphabet.
notes.gloss: The opinion that a long-deserted wife may be absolved of adultery.

notes.citation: Decretum Gratiani, c. Si tu abstines, C. 28 q. 2 again (the note is garbled in the print: eſt tabuſtines xxvij. c. ij.)
Novel 117 (Ut liceat matri et aviae, Authenticum coll. 8), c. 9, § Si ergo contigerit
notes.original: Paragra. Si ergo contigerit vt lic. ma. & auiæ. aux nouuelles de Iuſtiniẽ, ſous la collation vſ.
notes.gloss: The grounds on which a husband may repudiate his wife; the paragraph number and Coras's collation numeral ("vſ", elsewhere "vij") are not verified; the standard division puts Nov. 117 in the eighth collatio.

notes.original: L. Conſensu para. vir quoque. C. de rep
notes.gloss: Theodosius II and Valentinian III: a husband may repudiate a wife who, against his will, has passed the night outside his house.

notes.citation: Novel 117 c. 9, § Si ergo (the same paragraph as {d}), as an authentica
notes.gloss: Justinian: the husband who has himself turned his wife out cannot repudiate her for staying out.
